title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Maya Patel
body:
Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference's engineering SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and the canonical SRE runbook template. It consolidates existing practices into a single reference to ensure consistency across hosted, dedicated, and private offerings.

Goals

- Provide a clear, repeatable SLO lifecycle: definition, measurement, review, and action.
- Make error budget policy operational: known thresholds, responsible parties, and automated actions.
- Standardize capacity planning to meet throughput and latency SLOs with economical resource allocation.
- Define incident review standards that produce actionable remediation and regression controls.
- Publish a canonical runbook template and recommended tooling integrations.

Scope and Applicability

This standard applies to all externally-facing customer endpoints (API, SDK endpoints, embeddings, generation) and internal platform services that are critical for customer-facing inference (routing, runtime, KV cache, autoscaler, job-queue). Platform infra teams should apply the same practices to dedicated/private control planes and management services.

Key Definitions

- SLI (Service Level Indicator): A measurable signal of service health (e.g., p95 request latency, success rate, tokens/sec).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): A target for an SLI over a defined window (e.g., 99.95% availability over 30 days).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (the allowable fraction of failures or excess latency).
- Burn rate: Rate at which the error budget is consumed.

SLO Design Principles

1. Customer-centric metrics: Choose SLIs that reflect customer experience (successful responses, end-to-end latency for streaming, embeddings correctness).
2. Actionability: An SLO must trigger a concrete, documented action when breached or when the error budget burns rapidly.
3. Simplicity: Favor a small set (2-4) of SLOs per service: one availability, one latency, and optional correctness/quality SLOs for model output or embeddings.
4. Alignment: SLOs must align to product SLAs where applicable; enterprise contracts may define stricter SLOs handled as separate monitored objectives.
5. Observability: All SLOs must be backed by automated dashboards, alerts, and recorded in the SLO registry.

Standard SLOs and Example Targets

- Availability (success rate): 99.95% over 30 days (applies to REST and streaming connection establishment).
- Latency (inference tail latency): p95 < 250ms for small (<512 tokens) generation requests on hosted tier; p95 < 150ms on Dedicated when pinned to a high-throughput pool.
- Throughput / Capacity: Sustained throughput target of X tokens/sec per serving pool (defined per model family and machine class) - captured in capacity planning docs.
- Correctness (optional): Regression rate on evaluation prompt set <= 2% change vs. baseline for model rollouts.

Note: Services with enterprise SLAs should pin separate SLOs in the SLO registry and add a mapping in contracts.

SLO Registry and Ownership

- Each SLO must be recorded in the central SLO registry with: service, SLI definition (query/display), window (30d/7d/1d as appropriate), target, owner (team), and runbook link.
- Teams must review SLOs quarterly or after any major release that could impact quality/cost.

Error Budget Policy and Escalation

Error budget handling follows a three-tier policy: monitoring, mitigation, and risk control.

1) Monitoring
- Continuous burn monitoring with 6h, 24h, and 7d burn-rate calculations.
- Alerts:
  - Burn rate > 2x (6h window) -> notify on-call and SLO owner.
  - Burn rate > 5x (6h) or remaining budget < 10% -> trigger mitigation call (pager to SRE + service owner).
  - Remaining budget exhausted -> block non-essential launches and initiate rollback/rate-limiting plan.

2) Mitigation Playbook (automated and manual steps)
- Automated actions (where safe): redirect non-critical traffic to fallback model variants, increase autoscaler target within configured safety limits, enable conservative batching to reduce per-token pressure.
- Manual actions: rollback recent rollouts, throttle low-priority workloads (background re-ranking, internal batch jobs), contact product owners for launch holds.

3) Risk Control
- If remaining budget < 10% for 24+ hours, the service owner must open a remediation ticket with a target ETA and assign an action owner.
- Repeated exhaustion (3 occurrences in 90 days) triggers a Reliability Initiative (see section below).

Capacity Planning and Sizing Standards

Objectives:
- Ensure adequate headroom to meet SLOs during 99th percentile traffic surges while minimizing wasted reserved capacity.
- Provide a predictable contract between product launch plans and infra commitments for Dedicated/Private deployment customers.

Process (quarterly cadence with trigger-based reviews):
1. Ingest: collect traffic histograms (RPS, tokens/sec), request size distribution, sequence length profiles, and model-specific latency curves.
2. Baseline: identify steady-state capacity needed to meet p95/p99 latency targets with current batching and KV cache hit rates.
3. Stress margin: plan for N-day spike (default N = 3 business days), provisioned using a combination of reserved capacity + burst policies.
4. Cost optimization: apply quantization/instance family recommendations from Optimize team for long-running pools.
5. Publish: update the capacity plan artifact with expected headroom (% spare), risk notes, and scaling runbook.

Capacity Table (example template)

| Service | Model Family | Machine Class | Baseline TPS | p95 Latency Target | Headroom (%) | Owner | Notes |
|---------|--------------|---------------|--------------|--------------------|--------------|-------|-------|
| inference-api | redwood-1.2 | a2-highmem | 150 TPS | p95 < 250ms | 30% | eng-serving-runtime | KV cache hit 78% |

Reliability Initiatives (When to kick off)

- Repeated incident patterns tied to a single root cause (>=3 incidents with same RCA within 60 days).
- Recurrent error budget exhaustion (see policy).
- Near-miss analysis that reveals brittle failure modes.

Structure of an Initiative:
1. Sponsor and Champion (exec/senior eng)
2. Goal, success metrics, and timebox (typically 4-12 weeks)
3. Scope and out-of-scope list
4. Deliverables (code changes, autoscaler improvements, new observability panels, runbook updates)
5. Measurement plan (before/after SLOs, load tests)
6. Communication plan and retro

Incident Review and Postmortem Standards

All Sev1 and Sev2 incidents MUST have a postmortem published within 7 business days. Postmortems should follow this structure:

- Summary: brief incident timeline and impact (customer-visible metrics).
- Timeline: numbered timestamps with events and decisions.
- Root cause analysis: be specific (component, bug/config change, external dependency).
- Contributing factors: list systemic issues (observability gaps, unsafe defaults).
- Corrective actions: clear owner, ETA, and verification criteria.
- Learning and follow-ups: retro notes and documentation updates.
- Error budget impact and whether policy actions were invoked.

Postmortem quality checks (PR checklist):
- Does the postmortem identify a tangible RCA?
- Are corrective actions specific and timeboxed?
- Is there a verification plan?
- Has the related runbook been updated?

Runbook Standards and Template

Runbooks are the primary operational artifact that on-call engineers use to triage and mitigate incidents. Each monitored service must have a runbook that follows this template and be stored in the team-runbooks directory.

Runbook template (plain text)

Title: <service name> runbook
Owner: <team> | On-call: <pager duty schedule>
SLOs: <link to SLO entry>
Pager Symptoms: <alerts that page>
Customer Impact: <user-visible impact>
Metrics to check: <list of dashboards/queries>
Immediate Triage Steps (ordered):
1) Verify alert validity (are metrics reporting correctly?)
2) Check recent deployments and rollout windows (git tags, canary progress)
3) Inspect autoscaler and pool capacity (instances, GPU utilization, queue length)
4) Validate KV cache health and hit rate
5) If latency/availability degradation persists: toggle safe automated mitigations (fallback models, rate limit non-essential routes)
6) If root cause unclear: escalate to service owner and open an incident command channel

Mitigation Playbooks (examples)

- High p95 latency: 1) Confirm KV cache hit rate; 2) Increase batcher max latency threshold; 3) Scale target pool +10% (within safety limit); 4) Enable fallback model.
- Error rate spike for a model: 1) Rollback model version if recent change; 2) Route small percentage of traffic to older variant; 3) Open regression ticket and alert model team.

Operational Tooling and Integrations

Recommended stack and how we use it: 
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term retention; all SLO SLIs implemented as recorded Prometheus queries.
- Alerting: Alertmanager routed to PagerDuty with escalation policies mapped to SLO owners.
- Dashboards: Grafana (per-service SLO dashboard template).
- Incident channels: Slack + Incident Commander playbook (zoom/meet links in runbook).
- SLO registry: internal service (HTTP API) + UI with SLO metadata and links to runbooks/postmortems.
- Automation: CI jobs that run synthetic tests (canaries) and annotate SLO registry with results.

CLI and Query Examples (Prometheus style)

- Availability SLI (success rate):
  sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api",code!~"5.."}[30d])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference-api"}[30d]))

- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="inference-api"}[5m])) by (le))

- 6h burn rate computation pattern: (error_budget_burned_over_6h) / (error_budget_total)

Ownership, Reviews and Change Process

- SLO owner: the team that owns the customer-facing behavior. They are responsible for SLO registration, runbook maintenance, and remediation tracking.
- Quarterly SLO review: teams must present current SLOs, burn history, and capacity plans during the SRE quarterly review.
- Launch process: any feature or model rollout that can materially affect SLOs requires an SLO impact assessment and an approved risk mitigation plan before production rollout.

Verification and Auditing

- SLO registry audits run monthly to verify: owner contact, runbook link, and that the SLI query matches dashboard widgets.
- Incident review audits check that corrective actions were implemented and verified within promised ETAs.

Appendix A - Example Runbook (snippet)

---
Title: inference-api runbook
Owner: eng-serving-runtime | On-call: inference-pager
SLOs: 99.95% success rate (30d), p95 latency < 250ms
Pager Symptoms: high error-rate alert, p95-latency-exceeding threshold
Metrics to check:
- http_requests_total (by code)
- http_request_duration_seconds (p95/p99)
- queue_length, gpu_utilization, batcher_pending_requests
Immediate Triage Steps:
1) Check Grafana SLO dashboard (links)
2) Confirm whether a recent deployment is in progress (CI/CD pipeline)
3) Check autoscaler events (last 1h)
4) If error rate is high and no deployment: reduce traffic to suspected model via routing policy to a fallback

Appendix B - SLO Examples Table

| Service | SLI | Window | Target | Owner | Runbook |
| inference-api | success rate (http 2xx/3xx) | 30d | 99.95% | eng-serving-runtime | /runbooks/inference-api |
| embeddings | median embed latency | 30d | p95 < 120ms | eng-serving-runtime | /runbooks/embeddings |
